title: Robertson–Walker spaces
one_line_summary: Drops the spatial-flatness assumption of Chapter 15: symmetry alone fixes the curvature of each constant-time slice to a single constant, which yields the Robertson–Walker metric with k = +1, 0, -1; the chapter then explores the three geometries through proper distance, circumference-to-radius ratios, triangles and embeddings, derives the cosmological redshift 1+z = a(t_ob)/a(t_em) from null rays, and flags the Big-Bang singularity where a(t) vanishes.
role_in_book: Second chapter of Part III (Cosmology). Chapter 15 argued from homogeneity and isotropy for a metric of the form -dt^2 + a^2 gamma_ij dx^i dx^j and studied two spatially flat toy universes (Universe 0 and the de Sitter Universe 1). This chapter supplies the general spatial geometry allowed by those symmetries while deliberately leaving the matter side of Einstein's equation untouched: it is pure kinematics and geometry. It hands Chapter 17 (Friedmann equations) the metric, the curvature index k and the Ricci components needed to insert matter, gives Chapter 18 the redshift as the link between models and observation, and plants the initial singularity and the conformal (Poincaré disc) picture that Chapter 19 develops. The classical curvature of spheres and hyperbolic surfaces is treated properly only in Part V (Chapter 30) and Appendix D, so here those ideas are used intuitively.

assumed_background.topic: Homogeneity and isotropy leading to the metric form -dt^2 + a(t)^2 gamma_ij dx^i dx^j; Universes 0 and 1; Hubble parameter
Symmetries of the Riemann tensor and contraction to Ricci tensor and scalar
Connection coefficients computed from a metric
Gravitational redshift and the special-relativistic Doppler shift
Circles and triangles on a 2-sphere, Girard's theorem
Metric compatibility g_{mu nu; alpha} = 0 and the Bianchi identity (for exercises)
Spherical polar coordinates and line elements
Inverse trigonometric and hyperbolic functions, their integrals dr/sqrt(1-r^2) and dr/sqrt(1+r^2)
Wave period, frequency and wavelength relations
Hubble's observation that galaxies recede and light from them is redshifted

learning_objectives: Reader can explain why homogeneity and isotropy, not Einstein's equation, force the spatial Riemann tensor into the form K(gamma_ik gamma_jl - gamma_il gamma_jk) with a single constant K.
Reader can contract the constant-curvature Riemann tensor to obtain (3)R_jl = 2K gamma_jl and (3)R = 6K.
Reader can transform the isotropic form of the constant-curvature 3-metric into the areal-radius form dr^2/(1-Kr^2) + r^2 dOmega^2 by choosing r so that circumferences are 2 pi a r.
Reader can rescale K and r so that the curvature index k takes only the values +1, 0, -1 and a(t) carries dimensions of length, with K = k/a^2.
Reader can rewrite the Robertson–Walker metric using the hyperspherical coordinate chi with Sigma(chi) = sin chi, chi, sinh chi and state the allowed coordinate ranges.
Reader can compute the proper distance to a comoving galaxy for each k and derive Hubble's law v_p = H d_p from its time derivative.
Reader can use the ratio of proper circumference to proper radius, and triangle angle sums, to diagnose positive, zero or negative spatial curvature.

Reader can describe the embeddings of the k = +1 space as a 3-sphere in 4D Euclidean space and of the k = -1 space as a hyperboloid in 4D Minkowski space, and compute the volume 2 pi^2 a^3 of the closed universe.
Reader can distinguish flat space from flat spacetime: k = 0 with a varying a(t) is still curved spacetime.
Reader can derive the cosmological redshift 1+z = a(t_ob)/a(t_em) by comparing two successive null rays between comoving observers, and interpret it as wavelength stretching with a(t).
Reader can explain why a(t) -> 0 signals a curvature singularity (the Big Bang) at which classical GR ceases to apply.

teaching_approach.summary: A compact geometry-first chapter. It starts from what symmetry permits (one curvature number), finds the metric that realizes it, and then spends most of its effort making the three cases tangible with low-dimensional pictures: circles whose circumference falls short of or exceeds 2 pi times the radius, triangles with angle sums above or below pi, a sphere and a hyperboloid as embeddings, and the Poincaré disc. Much of the calculation is parked in boxed Examples and margin lists (connection coefficients, Ricci components) so that the main line stays short. The single physical payoff, the cosmological redshift, is derived with a visual integral-splitting trick. Matter and dynamics are explicitly deferred.
narrative_arc: Motivation: relax the spatial flatness of Chapter 15's toy universes while keeping homogeneity and isotropy; warn that time dependence can shrink space to a singular point.
Symmetry argument: the only tensor structure available for the spatial Riemann tensor is built from gamma_ij, so it must be K(gamma gamma - gamma gamma) with constant K; contract to Ricci and scalar.
Find the metric: quote the Robertson–Walker result for gamma_ij in isotropic coordinates, then (Example 16.1) change to a circumference-defined radius r to get dr^2/(1-Kr^2).
Normalize: rescale to k in {+1, 0, -1} and absorb |K| into a length-valued a(t); record the final RW line element.
Tabulate machinery: metric, vielbein, connection coefficients and Ricci components in the margin; introduce chi and Sigma(chi) in a boxed summary with coordinate ranges.
Measure distances: proper distance to a comoving galaxy for each k (Example 16.3, Fig. 16.1), differentiate to obtain Hubble's law.

Explore the three geometries in turn with a circumference-to-radius test, triangle area rules (Girard, Lambert), embeddings (Fig. 16.2), the Poincaré disc (Figs 16.3, 16.5), closed-universe volume and the round-trip light ray (Fig. 16.4).
Turn to observables: proper distance is not measurable, so derive the redshift from two successive null rays (Example 16.8, Fig. 16.6), interpret as wavelength stretching, define z.
Close by running time backwards: a -> 0 gives diverging density and curvature, the initial singularity, deferred to Chapter 19 and later.
signature_moves: Fixing the form of the curvature tensor by symmetry before ever writing down a metric, then asking which metric produces it.
Choosing the radial coordinate by an operational demand (circumference equals 2 pi times scale factor times r) rather than by algebraic convenience.
Using the same diagnostic, circumference over radius, for all three k values so the geometry becomes a comparison of one number with 2 pi.
Recycling two-dimensional results (Girard's theorem from Chapter 3, embeddings from Appendix D) as stand-ins for the three-dimensional spaces.
Reading Lambert's hyperbolic triangle formula as Girard's formula on a sphere of imaginary radius to make negative curvature feel like a continuation of positive curvature.
A playful hook (seeing the back of your own head) to make the angle-like radial coordinate of the closed universe memorable, with a margin caveat that real models do not allow it.
Splitting two integrals so their common middle cancels, illustrated by a two-ray timing diagram, to reduce the redshift derivation to one line.
Relegating component lists (connection coefficients, Ricci) to margins so the prose argument stays uncluttered while the data remain available for the next chapter.

sections.title: Chapter opening: beyond spatially flat universes
sections.summary: After an epigraph from C. S. Peirce, the authors explain that they will now allow the spatial slices of a homogeneous, isotropic universe to be curved, producing geometries that are only the left-hand side of Einstein's equation; matter comes next chapter. They preview that the curvature is constant and can be positive, zero or negative, and that time dependence lets all three shrink to a point where spacetime curvature diverges, which they connect to the Big Bang. Margin notes define constant curvature and recall how a ball's circles tear or a saddle's circles fold when flattened.
key_moves: Frame the chapter as geometry only, deferring matter to Chapter 17.
Preview the three curvature classes by sign.
Announce the singularity as a consequence of a shrinking scale factor rather than of any specific matter content.

sections.title: Spaces with constant curvature
sections.summary: Starting from the symmetry-based metric form of Chapter 15, the section argues that the Riemann tensor of the spatial slices can only be K times an antisymmetrized product of the 3-metric, contracts it to (3)R_jl = 2K gamma_jl and (3)R = 6K, and quotes Robertson and Walker's unique metric in isotropic coordinates. Example 16.1 changes to a radius defined by circumference, rescales to k = +1, 0, -1 with a(t) now a length, and produces the Robertson–Walker line element. Example 16.2 motivates the chi coordinate by analogy with the 2-spaces of Appendix D, and margins list metric, vielbein, connection coefficients and orthonormal Ricci components. A boxed summary gives the chi form with Sigma(chi) and coordinate ranges, emphasizing that chi is bounded only for k = +1. A margin note separates constant spatial curvature from constant spacetime curvature.
concepts: three-dimensional Riemann tensor of spatial slices
connection coefficients of the Robertson–Walker metric
key_moves: Only gamma_ij can build an isotropic, homogeneous rank-4 tensor with Riemann symmetries, giving eqn 16.2.
Contract with gamma^ik using gamma^ik gamma_ik = 3 to get Ricci 2K gamma_jl.
Substitute r = R/(1 + KR^2/4) so that the angular part reads a^2 r^2 dOmega^2.
Set k = K/|K|, r-bar = |K|^{1/2} r and redefine a -> a/sqrt|K|, so K = k/a^2.
Replace r by chi via dchi^2 = dr^2/(1-kr^2): r = sin chi, chi, sinh chi.
Note that chi runs only to pi for k = +1, hinting at a finite space.

sections.title: Proper distance and Hubble's law (Example 16.3)
sections.summary: With coordinates comoving and t the cosmic time, the proper distance on a constant-time slice from the origin to a galaxy at fixed coordinate xi is a(t) times arcsin xi, xi, or arsinh xi for k = +1, 0, -1 (Fig. 16.1). For k = +1 the distance reaches a finite value pi a/2 as xi approaches 1. Differentiating in time, the xi-dependent factor is just l/a in every case, so the rate of change of proper distance is H times proper distance: Hubble's law, valid for all three geometries.
concepts: proper distance in a Robertson–Walker spacetime
key_moves: Integrate the radial line element at fixed t.
Observe that the comoving factor is time independent, so d l/dt = (da/dt)(l/a).
Identify H = (1/a) da/dt and read the result as v_p = H d_p.

sections.title: Three Robertson–Walker spaces: the circumference test and k = 0
sections.summary: The section proposes to compare the proper circumference of a circle with its proper radius for each k, reusing the tearing-versus-folding picture from the opening margin note. For k = 0 the metric is Chapter 15's Universe 1 form; with constant a the spacetime is Minkowski, but with time-varying a the flat space expands and the spacetime is curved. Example 16.4 confirms the ratio is exactly 2 pi and ties the case to Euclidean parallels and angle sums of pi.
key_moves: Circumference of a coordinate circle of radius xi is 2 pi a xi for every k.
Proper radius differs by k, so the ratio encodes curvature.
Distinguish spatial flatness from spacetime flatness through the time dependence of a.

sections.title: The case k = +1: closed spherical space
sections.summary: The k = +1 spatial metric embeds in four-dimensional Euclidean space as a 3-sphere of radius a (margin eqn 16.28, Fig. 16.2a). Example 16.5 connects the geometry to the surface of a 2-sphere: parallel geodesics meet, triangle angles exceed pi with Girard's area rule, and the circumference-to-radius ratio is below 2 pi. The volume integral over 0 <= chi <= pi gives 2 pi^2 a^3, so the space is closed yet has no edge or centre, like a 2-sphere experienced from within. Example 16.6 notes that chi acts like an angle, so a radial light ray can circle the whole universe and in principle return to its origin, a possibility later ruled out for realistic models.
key_moves: Embed the slice in flat R^4 with the fourth coordinate equal to a cos chi and the other three equal to a sin chi times the usual unit-vector direction factors.
Ratio 2 pi xi / arcsin xi <= 2 pi.
Volume element 4 pi a^3 sin^2 chi dchi integrated to 2 pi^2 a^3.
Closed means finite volume, not bounded by an edge.
Radial null rays wrap around the chi circle.

sections.title: The case k = -1: open hyperbolic space
sections.summary: The k = -1 spatial metric embeds, as a whole, only in four-dimensional Minkowski space, as one sheet of the hyperboloid w^2 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2 = a^2 (margin eqn 16.33, Fig. 16.2b). Example 16.7 names the geometry hyperbolic: parallels diverge, triangle angles fall short of pi and Lambert's formula gives the area, which looks like Girard's rule on a sphere of imaginary radius. The Poincaré disc (Figs 16.3b, 16.5) is introduced as a projection of the hyperboloid in which geodesics hit the rim at right angles. The circumference ratio exceeds 2 pi; the volume diverges because chi is unbounded, so the space is called open, with a margin caution that k = 0 is also open. (The book twice calls the embedded surface a '2-sheet hyperboloid'; only one sheet, w > 0, is the spatial slice.)
key_moves: Embed via w = a cosh chi, spatial coordinates a sinh chi times angular factors.
Lambert area = R^2(pi - sum of angles), read as a sphere with R^2 -> -R^2.
Ratio 2 pi xi / arsinh xi >= 2 pi.
Infinite volume since chi ranges to infinity.

sections.title: Redshift and cosmic expansion
sections.summary: Because proper distances cannot be measured directly, the section turns to the redshift, the third kind after Doppler and gravitational shifts. A comoving observer at the origin receives light from a comoving galaxy; radial null rays obey dt = a dr/sqrt(1-kr^2). Example 16.8 writes this for two successive wave crests, splits the time integrals so that the long common interval cancels (Fig. 16.6), and uses the shortness of the period to conclude delta t_em / a(t_em) = delta t_ob / a(t_ob). Converting periods to frequencies gives omega_ob/omega_em = a(t_em)/a(t_ob), depending only on the scale factor at the two events; Example 16.9 notes redshift for expansion and blueshift for contraction. Wavelength therefore scales with a, which (in a margin note) also holds for neutrinos and gravitational waves. The redshift parameter z is defined, giving 1+z = a(t_ob)/a(t_em), or 1/a(t_em) with today's a set to one.
concepts: radial null geodesic in a Robertson–Walker spacetime
wavelength stretching with the scale factor
key_moves: Set ds^2 = 0 for a radial ray and separate variables.
The comoving coordinate integral is the same for both crests because emitter and observer are comoving.
Split the time integrals and cancel the shared piece from t_em + delta t_em to t_ob.
Treat 1/a as constant over one period to linearize.
Invert periods to frequencies, then to wavelengths, and define z.

sections.title: The initial singularity
sections.summary: A short qualitative closing section. Once matter is added (next chapter), density falls as the universe expands; running the models backwards, most reach a(t) = 0 a finite time ago, where the density grows without bound. Because matter sources the metric, this is not only a density blow-up (as in a Newtonian model) but a divergence of spacetime curvature that classical GR cannot handle, so the point must be excised: the Big Bang, the initial singularity. The authors defer its treatment as an edge of spacetime to Chapter 19.
key_moves: Reverse the direction of time in an expanding model.
Contrast a Newtonian density singularity with a GR curvature singularity.
Excise the singular point from the spacetime description.

sections.title: Chapter summary
sections.summary: Three bullet points restate that there are three homogeneous, isotropic Robertson–Walker geometries labelled by k, that their evolution through a(t) is tied to observed redshift by 1+z = a(t_ob)/a(t_em), and that these universes may begin in a Big-Bang singularity.
key_moves: Restate eqn 16.49 (metric) and eqn 16.50 (redshift).

concepts.name: cosmological principle
concepts.definition: The assumption that, on large scales, space looks the same at every location (homogeneity) and in every direction (isotropy) at a given cosmic time.
concepts.how_introduced: Carried over from Chapter 15, where it produced the general form of the cosmological metric; here it is used to forbid any preferred direction in the spatial curvature tensor.
concepts.notes: The authors stress that the metric form follows from symmetry alone, independently of GR.

concepts.name: Robertson–Walker metric
concepts.definition: The most general metric of a spacetime whose constant-time spatial slices are homogeneous and isotropic: ds^2 = -dt^2 + a(t)^2 [dr^2/(1-kr^2) + r^2 dOmega^2], with k = +1, 0 or -1 and scale factor a(t).
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by first fixing the spatial curvature by symmetry, quoting the unique metric with that curvature, changing to a circumference-based radius and rescaling so k takes three values.
concepts.notes: The book does not mention Friedmann or Lemaître in this chapter; the geometry is independent of the field equations.

concepts.name: scale factor
concepts.definition: The function a(t) multiplying the spatial part of the Robertson–Walker metric; proper distances between comoving points are proportional to it. After rescaling for k = ±1 it has dimensions of length and the spatial curvature is K = k/a^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Inherited from Chapter 15 as a dimensionless factor, then redefined in Example 16.1 by absorbing 1/sqrt|K| so that it becomes a length, which motivates calling it the radius of the universe by analogy with a sphere.
concepts.notes: For k = 0 there is no natural normalization; later the book sets a(t_ob) = 1.

concepts.name: cosmic time
concepts.definition: The time coordinate t of the Robertson–Walker metric, equal to the proper time kept by comoving observers (g_tt = -1), labelling the homogeneous spatial slices.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in passing when the authors note the RW coordinates are comoving; relied on in the redshift derivation where coordinate intervals are treated as proper periods.

concepts.name: comoving coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates in which galaxies moving with the cosmic expansion have fixed spatial labels (r, theta, phi) or (chi, theta, phi); all expansion is carried by a(t).
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted for the RW coordinates with a margin reminder of the Chapter 15 conditions on metric derivatives; used to define fixed comoving separation xi and to argue that two light crests traverse the same coordinate interval.

concepts.name: three-dimensional Riemann tensor of spatial slices
aliases: intrinsic curvature of the constant-t hypersurface
concepts.definition: The Riemann tensor built from the 3-metric gamma_ij of a constant-time hypersurface alone, describing the intrinsic curvature of space (not spacetime) at that instant.
concepts.how_introduced: Constructed to classify spatial geometries: homogeneity and isotropy leave gamma_ij as the only building block, and Riemann symmetries then allow a single arrangement with one constant.
concepts.notes: A margin note mentions that the Levi-Civita symbol is the only other isotropic 3-tensor, but it is not needed.

concepts.name: space of constant curvature
concepts.definition: A space whose Riemann tensor has the form K(g_ik g_jl - g_il g_jk) with the same K at every point, so its curvature is characterized by a single number and looks identical in all places and directions.
concepts.how_introduced: Reached by the symmetry argument for the spatial slices; named once the matching metric (eqn 16.5) is found. Exercise 16.5 asks for the proof (via the Bianchi identity) that isotropy at each point forces the coefficient to be constant.
prerequisites: three-dimensional Riemann tensor of spatial slices
concepts.notes: The constancy result is Schur's theorem, though the book does not name it.

concepts.name: Gaussian curvature
aliases: sectional curvature of the spatial slice
concepts.definition: For these spaces, the constant K in the constant-curvature Riemann tensor, with dimensions of inverse length squared; for a 2-sphere of radius r it equals +1/r^2, and it is negative for hyperbolic geometry.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the coefficient in eqn 16.2 with only a pointer to Chapter 30 for its classical meaning; its sign is identified with spherical, flat or hyperbolic geometry using the sphere example.
prerequisites: three-dimensional Riemann tensor of spatial slices
concepts.notes: The classical (surface) meaning of Gaussian curvature is deferred to Chapter 30, Classical curvature; in this chapter K is used as a label whose sign sets the geometry.

concepts.name: curvature index k
concepts.definition: The sign of the spatial curvature, k = K/|K| for K nonzero and k = 0 otherwise, taking values +1 (spherical, closed), 0 (flat) and -1 (hyperbolic, open) after rescaling r and a.
concepts.how_introduced: Produced by rescaling in Example 16.1 to strip dimensions from the bracketed part of the metric.

concepts.name: spatial Ricci tensor and scalar
concepts.definition: Contractions of the spatial Riemann tensor: for constant curvature, (3)R_jl = 2K gamma_jl and (3)R = 6K.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by a one-line contraction using gamma^ik gamma_ik = 3; a margin caution stresses these are not the spacetime quantities that enter Einstein's equation.
prerequisites: three-dimensional Riemann tensor of spatial slices

concepts.name: isotropic coordinates for constant-curvature space
concepts.definition: A coordinate system in which the constant-curvature 3-metric is a position-dependent multiple of the Euclidean metric: gamma_ij = [1 + K(x^2+y^2+z^2)/4]^{-2} delta_ij.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted as Robertson and Walker's unique solution matching eqn 16.2, then converted to polar form (eqn 16.8) before the change to an areal radius.
concepts.notes: Geometrically this is stereographic projection; the book does not use that name.

concepts.name: areal radial coordinate
concepts.definition: A radial coordinate r chosen so that the angular part of the metric is a^2 r^2 dOmega^2, making the proper circumference of a coordinate circle equal to 2 pi a r (and sphere area 4 pi a^2 r^2), at the cost of a non-trivial g_rr.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated operationally in Example 16.1 by demanding that circumferences look Euclidean, leading to r = R/(1 + KR^2/4).
concepts.notes: For k = +1 this r reaches a maximum of 1 and then retraces, so it covers only half of the 3-sphere at a time.

concepts.name: hyperspherical radial coordinate chi
concepts.definition: A dimensionless radial coordinate defined by dchi = dr/sqrt(1-kr^2), so that r = Sigma(chi) with Sigma = sin chi, chi, sinh chi for k = +1, 0, -1; the spatial metric becomes dchi^2 + Sigma^2 dOmega^2. It ranges over [0, pi] for k = +1 and [0, infinity) otherwise.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated in Example 16.2 by the 2-space analysis of Appendix D and presented in a boxed summary as the most useful coordinates for applications.
concepts.notes: Proper radial distance on a slice is simply a chi; for k = +1, chi behaves like a polar angle on a 3-sphere.

concepts.name: connection coefficients of the Robertson–Walker metric
concepts.definition: The non-zero Christoffel symbols and orthonormal Ricci components of the RW metric, e.g. Gamma^t_rr = a adot/(1-kr^2), Gamma^i_tj = (adot/a) delta^i_j, R_tt-hat = -3 addot/a, R_ii-hat = addot/a + 2 adot^2/a^2 + 2k/a^2, R = 6(addot/a + adot^2/a^2 + k/a^2).
concepts.how_introduced: Listed without derivation in the margin of Example 16.2 as the data needed to insert the metric into Einstein's equation; Exercise 16.3 asks for verification.
concepts.notes: The printed spatial Ricci component has 2k/a where 2k/a^2 is required by dimensions and by the trace; see gaps.

concepts.name: spacetime of constant curvature
concepts.definition: A four-dimensional spacetime whose Riemann tensor is a fixed constant C times the antisymmetrized product of two copies of the spacetime metric (the same structure as the spatial case), which implies Ricci equal to one quarter of the Ricci scalar times the metric; de Sitter spacetime is an example.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised in a margin note to warn that the constant spatial curvature of RW slices is a different statement from the constant spacetime curvature of Universe 1; linked via Exercises 16.5 and 16.6.

concepts.name: flat Robertson–Walker universe
concepts.definition: The k = 0 case, whose constant-time slices are ordinary Euclidean 3-space scaled by a(t); it is infinite (open) and its circles have circumference exactly 2 pi times their radius.
concepts.how_introduced: The first of the three cases in §16.2, identified with Chapter 15's Universe 1 metric form and with the Euclidean plane (Example 16.4).

concepts.name: flat space versus flat spacetime
aliases: spatial flatness is not spacetime flatness
concepts.definition: Spatial slices can be intrinsically flat while the four-dimensional spacetime is curved: for k = 0 the Riemann tensor vanishes only if a(t) is constant.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated when discussing k = 0: constant a gives Minkowski space, time-dependent a gives an expanding flat space in a curved spacetime.
concepts.notes: Visible directly in the Ricci scalar 6(addot/a + adot^2/a^2 + k/a^2).

concepts.name: closed spherical universe
concepts.definition: The k = +1 case: each spatial slice is a 3-sphere of radius a(t), with finite volume 2 pi^2 a^3, positive curvature, circles whose circumference is less than 2 pi times their radius, and no edge or centre.
concepts.how_introduced: Explored in §16.2 via embedding in 4D Euclidean space, analogies with the 2-sphere (Example 16.5), the finite range of chi and the round-the-universe light ray (Example 16.6).
concepts.notes: The book equates closed with k = +1; nontrivial topologies (e.g. a flat torus) are not discussed.

concepts.name: open hyperbolic universe
concepts.definition: The k = -1 case: each slice is a 3-dimensional hyperbolic space of curvature -1/a^2, infinite in volume, in which parallel geodesics diverge, triangle angles sum to less than pi and circles have circumference exceeding 2 pi times their radius.
concepts.how_introduced: Explored in §16.2 via embedding as a hyperboloid in 4D Minkowski space, Lambert's triangle formula and the Poincaré disc (Example 16.7).
concepts.notes: A margin caution notes that 'open' is ambiguous because the flat case is also infinite.

concepts.name: embedding of spatial sections
concepts.definition: Representing a curved 3-space as a hypersurface in a flat 4-dimensional space whose induced metric reproduces the spatial RW metric: a sphere in Euclidean R^4 for k = +1, a hyperboloid in Minkowski space for k = -1.
concepts.how_introduced: Given via explicit parametrizations in margin eqns 16.28 and 16.33 and drawn with one dimension suppressed in Fig. 16.2; full treatment deferred to Appendix D.
concepts.notes: Only portions of hyperbolic space embed in Euclidean space; the whole needs a Minkowski ambient space.

concepts.name: circumference-to-radius curvature test
concepts.definition: An intrinsic diagnostic of curvature: compare the proper circumference of a circle with its proper radius; the ratio equals 2 pi in flat space, is smaller for positive curvature and larger for negative curvature.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced by the opening margin note (a ball tears when flattened, a saddle folds) and applied to all three RW spaces in eqns 16.26, 16.30 and 16.35.
prerequisites: proper distance in a Robertson–Walker spacetime

concepts.name: angle sum of geodesic triangles
concepts.definition: In a curved 2-geometry the interior angles of a triangle made from geodesics sum to more than pi (positive curvature), exactly pi (flat) or less than pi (negative curvature), with the difference proportional to area.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the second qualitative marker of each geometry in Examples 16.4, 16.5 and 16.7, with pictures in Fig. 16.3.

concepts.name: Girard's theorem
concepts.definition: The area of a geodesic triangle on a sphere of radius R is R^2 times the excess of its angle sum over pi.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 3 in Example 16.5 as the 2D model for positive curvature.

concepts.name: Lambert's formula for hyperbolic triangles
concepts.definition: The area of a geodesic triangle in a hyperbolic plane with curvature -1/R^2 equals R^2 times the deficit of the angle sum below pi.
concepts.how_introduced: Given in Example 16.7 and interpreted as Girard's theorem on a sphere of imaginary radius sqrt(-R^2), signalling negative curvature.

concepts.name: Poincaré disc model
concepts.definition: A representation of the entire hyperbolic plane inside a unit disc, obtained by projecting the hyperboloid; it preserves angles (conformal), and geodesics are diameters or circular arcs meeting the boundary circle at right angles.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown in Fig. 16.3(b) to display a hyperbolic triangle and in Fig. 16.5 as a projection of the hyperboloid; margin note flags it as conformal and credits Beltrami.
concepts.notes: Conformal representations return in Chapter 19 (causal structure).

concepts.name: volume of the closed universe
concepts.definition: The total proper volume of a k = +1 spatial slice, 2 pi^2 a(t)^3, finite because chi runs from 0 to pi.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed by integrating 4 pi a^3 sin^2 chi dchi; used to justify the name closed and contrasted with the divergent k = -1 volume.

concepts.name: proper distance in a Robertson–Walker spacetime
concepts.definition: The length measured along a constant-cosmic-time slice between two comoving points, l(t) = a(t) chi, which equals a arcsin xi, a xi or a arsinh xi in terms of the areal coordinate xi for k = +1, 0, -1.
concepts.how_introduced: Built in Example 16.3 by integrating the radial line element; plotted as l/a in Fig. 16.1 and later declared not directly measurable.
concepts.notes: It is defined on a hypersurface of simultaneity that no single observer can survey.

concepts.name: Hubble parameter
concepts.definition: The fractional rate of change of the scale factor, H = (1/a) da/dt.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 15 and identified as the proportionality constant in the time derivative of proper distance.

concepts.name: Hubble's law
concepts.definition: In any RW spacetime, the rate of change of proper distance to a comoving galaxy is proportional to that distance: v_p = H(t) d_p.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by differentiating the proper distances of Example 16.3 and noticing that the comoving factor equals l/a for all k.
prerequisites: proper distance in a Robertson–Walker spacetime
concepts.notes: The book does not discuss that v_p exceeds c beyond d = c/H; this is not a violation of relativity.

concepts.name: radial null geodesic in a Robertson–Walker spacetime
concepts.definition: A light signal moving radially (fixed theta, phi) satisfies dt = ± a(t) dr/sqrt(1-kr^2), so the comoving coordinate it covers is the integral of dt/a.
concepts.how_introduced: Written in §16.3 for crests travelling from a comoving galaxy to an observer at the origin.

concepts.name: comoving distance
concepts.definition: The time-independent coordinate separation covered by light, eta = integral of dt/a from emission to observation, equal to chi for the source; multiplying by a(t) gives the (time-dependent) proper distance.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in margin note 18 while setting up the redshift derivation.
prerequisites: radial null geodesic in a Robertson–Walker spacetime
concepts.notes: Many texts use eta for conformal time; here it denotes the comoving distance the ray covers, numerically the same integral.

concepts.name: cosmological redshift
concepts.definition: The shift of light to lower frequency (for expansion) between comoving emitter and observer, fixed only by the scale factor at emission and observation: omega_ob/omega_em = a(t_em)/a(t_ob).
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated as the only practical way to measure a(t) since rulers cannot measure expansion; derived by comparing two successive crests along radial null rays and cancelling a shared interval.
prerequisites: radial null geodesic in a Robertson–Walker spacetime
concepts.notes: Contracting universes give a blueshift by the same formula.

concepts.name: redshift parameter z
concepts.definition: The fractional increase in wavelength, z = (lambda_ob - lambda_em)/lambda_em; in RW cosmology 1+z = a(t_ob)/a(t_em), or 1/a(t_em) when today's scale factor is set to one.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined immediately after the frequency result; the zero of time is often chosen where z would be infinite, a = 0.
prerequisites: wavelength stretching with the scale factor

concepts.name: wavelength stretching with the scale factor
concepts.definition: Wavelengths of freely propagating radiation grow in proportion to a(t), as if printed on space that stretches; the same scaling holds for neutrinos and gravitational waves.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as an intuitive rereading of the frequency ratio; a margin note extends it beyond photons.

concepts.name: three causes of redshift
concepts.definition: Frequency shifts of light can arise from relative motion (Doppler), from climbing out of a gravitational potential, and from the expansion of the universe between emission and reception.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed at the start of §16.3 to position the cosmological shift as new; a margin box points forward to Chapter 22 for the gravitational case.

concepts.name: initial singularity
concepts.definition: The moment, a finite time in the past for most expanding models, at which a(t) = 0, the density diverges and spacetime curvature becomes infinite, so the point is removed from the spacetime and no known law applies.
concepts.how_introduced: Previewed in the opening and discussed qualitatively in §16.4 by running an expanding, matter-filled model backwards; its treatment as an edge of spacetime is deferred to Chapter 19.
concepts.notes: Revisited in Chapter 50, 'The Big-Bang singularity'.

concepts.name: curvature singularity
concepts.definition: A place where curvature invariants of spacetime diverge, so the metric field itself breaks down and cannot be continued by a coordinate change.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted in §16.4 with a Newtonian singularity, where only density blows up: in GR the density sources the metric, so the geometry itself fails.

concepts.name: redshift drift
concepts.definition: The slow change in a source's redshift as the observer's time advances, related to the expansion rates at emission and observation by H(t_em) = H(t_ob)(1+z) - dz/dt_ob.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears only in Exercise 16.9.

figures.label: Fig. 16.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Proper distance divided by scale factor, plotted against the comoving areal coordinate xi for the three curvature cases.
figures.visual_description: Axes: horizontal xi (arrow to the right), vertical l(t)/a(t). A dotted horizontal line marks the level 1. Three curves start together at the origin with a common slope of 1: a straight line labelled xi (flat), a curve that falls slightly below it labelled sinh^-1 xi (hyperbolic), and a curve that bends above both labelled sin^-1 xi (spherical), steepening sharply near the top of the plot where xi approaches 1.
figures.what_it_teaches: For small separations all geometries agree (local flatness); at larger xi the same areal coordinate corresponds to more proper distance in a closed space and less in an open space, and the k = +1 areal coordinate has a hard limit at xi = 1.
concepts: proper distance in a Robertson–Walker spacetime

redesign.idea: Paired plot and embedded surface: a slider for xi moves a circle outward on a sphere, a plane and a hyperbolic disc; the plot shows l/a and circumference/(2 pi a) simultaneously so learners see where r stops being a good label on the sphere (the equator).
redesign.interaction: Drag xi or a marker on the surface; toggle k; optionally plot chi instead of r on the horizontal axis to remove the vertical asymptote.

figures.label: Fig. 16.2(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: The k = +1 spatial universe drawn as a sphere in a flat four-dimensional Euclidean space with one angular direction dropped.
figures.visual_description: Small line drawing of a sphere centred on the origin of a three-axis frame labelled w (vertical, up), x (lower right) and y (lower left). The back halves of the axes are dashed inside the sphere; the sphere surface is outlined with light stippling.
figures.what_it_teaches: A closed spatial universe is the surface (not the interior) of a hypersphere of radius a; the embedding coordinate w is fictitious.

redesign.idea: 3D sphere whose radius is a(t) animated over time with comoving galaxy dots painted on the surface; a toggle shows that the interior and the w axis are scaffolding, not part of the universe.
redesign.interaction: Play/pause cosmic time; drag to rotate; click a galaxy to show geodesic distance a chi to others growing.

figures.label: Fig. 16.2(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: The k = -1 spatial universe drawn as a hyperboloid sheet in four-dimensional Minkowski space with one angular direction dropped.
figures.visual_description: A bowl-shaped surface opening upward, with its lowest point (labelled a) sitting on the vertical w axis above the origin of an axis frame with x to the lower right and y to the lower left. Only one sheet (w > 0) is drawn.
figures.what_it_teaches: Negative spatial curvature can be realized as a hyperboloid w^2 - x^2 - y^2 = a^2 in a space with a Minkowski-signature metric; its lowest point is at distance a from the origin.

redesign.idea: Hyperboloid in 3D with a Minkowski light cone overlay; learners place a triangle of galaxies and see its angle sum and area computed, with a(t) growing over time.
redesign.interaction: Drag vertices along the surface; slider for a(t); toggle between Euclidean-looking rendering and a note that lengths use the Minkowski rule.

figures.label: Fig. 16.3(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: A geodesic triangle on a 2-sphere, whose angles add to more than pi.
figures.visual_description: Wire-frame sphere with several great circles drawn, some dashed on the far side. On the left-front face, three great-circle arcs bound a small cross-hatched triangle. (The inventory attaches the Fig. 16.2 label to this image; it actually shows Fig. 16.3(a).)
figures.what_it_teaches: Positive curvature: triangles made of great-circle geodesics have angle excess, related to area by Girard's theorem.

redesign.idea: Drag three vertices on a sphere; live readout of the three angles, their sum, the excess and R^2 times excess compared with the measured area.
redesign.interaction: Drag vertices; slider for sphere radius; shrink the triangle to watch the excess vanish.

figures.label: Fig. 16.3(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: A geodesic triangle in the Poincaré disc model of hyperbolic space, whose angles add to less than pi.
figures.visual_description: A circle (the disc boundary) containing a horizontal diameter and several circular arcs; small square markers show where arcs meet the rim at right angles. Three of these geodesics bound a slim, hatched triangle with concave sides near the centre-left.
figures.what_it_teaches: Negative curvature: hyperbolic triangles are thin with angle deficit; the disc model is conformal so the angles seen are the true angles.

redesign.idea: Poincaré disc sandbox: drag vertices, geodesic arcs orthogonal to the rim are drawn automatically, angle sum and pi-minus-sum times R^2 compared with numerically integrated area.
redesign.interaction: Drag vertices toward the rim to watch angles shrink toward zero and area approach pi R^2.

figures.label: Fig. 16.4(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: In a closed universe, radial light from star B ahead and from star C behind both arrive at observer A.
figures.visual_description: A circle representing the chi direction of the closed space. A dot A sits on the right, B a little higher on the upper right, C on the left. Just outside the circle a short arrowed arc runs from B down to A, while a long arrowed arc starts near C and wraps around the lower half of the circle to arrive at A from the other side.
figures.what_it_teaches: The radial coordinate chi behaves like an angle, so there are two radial routes between any two points and light can arrive from opposite directions.
concepts: radial null geodesic in a Robertson–Walker spacetime

redesign.idea: Animated circle universe (chi as angle) with a growing radius a(t): photons emitted from chosen stars travel at fixed d chi/dt = 1/a, arriving by both routes, each with the redshift set by a at emission and arrival.
redesign.interaction: Click to emit photons from any point; choose a(t) (static, linear, decelerating); readouts of arrival times and 1+z.

figures.label: Fig. 16.4(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Given enough time, a radial light ray could go all the way around a closed universe.
figures.visual_description: A circle with observer A on the right and a single long arrowed arc drawn just outside the circle that starts at A and runs all the way around, ending back at A with an arrowhead.
figures.what_it_teaches: Seeing the back of your own head: a closed space has no edge, so a straight path returns to its start.

redesign.idea: Extend the previous demo with a Friedmann-type a(t) that recollapses and plot comoving distance travelled by a photon against 2 pi to show whether a full lap is achievable before the big crunch.
redesign.interaction: Slider for density parameter; animate the lap fraction.

figures.label: Fig. 16.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Curves on a hyperboloid project down onto the Poincaré disc, where geodesics meet the boundary at right angles.
figures.visual_description: A cone drawn with bold dashed straight sides (the asymptotic light cone) opening upward, with a hyperboloid surface nested inside and labelled 'hyperboloid'. A dark curve lies on the hyperboloid. Thin straight projection lines run from points on the hyperboloid down through a flat elliptical disc labelled 'Poincaré disc' drawn below the cone's apex, converging toward a single point beneath the disc.
figures.what_it_teaches: The Poincaré disc is a projection of the hyperboloid through a fixed point below it; the whole infinite hyperbolic sheet maps into a finite disc, and the cone's rim maps to the disc boundary.

redesign.idea: Linked 3D/2D views: a hyperboloid with a draggable geodesic (plane-through-origin intersection) and its stereographic projection on the disc updating live; tiles of equal hyperbolic area shrink toward the rim.
redesign.interaction: Rotate the cutting plane; drag a point far up the hyperboloid and watch its image approach the rim.

figures.label: Fig. 16.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Timing picture for two successive crests: the long shared interval of comoving distance cancels, leaving one period at each end.
figures.visual_description: Vertical time axis implied. On the left a solid upward arrow runs from a tick labelled t_em to a tick labelled t_ob. On the right a second solid arrow runs from a lower tick labelled t_em + delta t_em to an upper tick labelled t_ob + delta t_ob. Between them a dashed arrow runs from the level of t_em + delta t_em up to the level of t_ob, with dashed horizontal lines joining the tick levels, marking the overlap interval.
figures.what_it_teaches: The integral of dt/a over [t_em, t_ob] and over the shifted interval share the dashed middle part; equating them leaves equal comoving distances for the short emission and reception windows. The caption misprints the second observation time as t_ob + delta t_em and 'common' as 'comment'.
concepts: radial null geodesic in a Robertson–Walker spacetime

redesign.idea: Spacetime diagram in (comoving distance, t) with a user-chosen a(t): two crests leave the source a period apart; shading the area under 1/a for each ray shows equal areas and the stretched arrival spacing, with 1+z readout.
redesign.interaction: Slider for emission period and expansion history; drag the source distance; watch the arrival period and the ratio a(t_ob)/a(t_em) match.

worked_examples.label: Example 16.1
worked_examples.problem: Put the constant-curvature RW metric (isotropic coordinates) into a form whose angular part is Euclidean-looking, then normalize the curvature to three values.
worked_examples.method: Write in Cartesian and polar isotropic form; define r = R/(1 + KR^2/4) so the angular term is a^2 r^2 dOmega^2; verify g_rr becomes 1/(1-Kr^2); rescale r-bar = |K|^{1/2} r, k = K/|K| and absorb 1/sqrt|K| into a.
worked_examples.key_insight: Choosing the radial coordinate by the circumference it gives makes curvature appear only in g_rr, and the curvature magnitude can be hidden inside a length-valued a(t), leaving just its sign k.
worked_examples.result: ds^2 = -dt^2 + a^2[dr^2/(1-kr^2) + r^2 dOmega^2] with k = +1, 0, -1 and K = k/a^2.

worked_examples.label: Example 16.2
worked_examples.problem: Relate the three RW spaces to the 2-spaces of Appendix D, remove the factor 1-kr^2 with a new radial variable, and record metric, vielbein, connection and Ricci data.
worked_examples.method: Analogy with sphere and two-sheet hyperboloid; substitute dchi^2 = dr^2/(1-kr^2) with r = sin chi, chi, sinh chi; list components in the margin (both r and chi forms).
worked_examples.key_insight: The same radial function Sigma(chi) encodes all three curvatures, and the RW Ricci components depend only on addot/a, (adot/a)^2 and k/a^2.
worked_examples.result: Boxed chi form (16.15)-(16.17); R = 6(addot/a + adot^2/a^2 + k/a^2).
concepts: connection coefficients of the Robertson–Walker metric

worked_examples.label: Example 16.3
worked_examples.problem: Find the proper distance at cosmic time t to a comoving galaxy at areal coordinate xi, and how fast it changes.
worked_examples.method: Integrate a dr/sqrt(1-kr^2) from 0 to xi for each k, then differentiate with respect to t holding xi fixed.
worked_examples.key_insight: Because the comoving part is time independent, every proper distance grows at the same fractional rate adot/a regardless of curvature, which is Hubble's law.
worked_examples.result: l = a arcsin xi, a xi, a arsinh xi; dl/dt = H l, i.e. v_p = H d_p.
concepts: proper distance in a Robertson–Walker spacetime

worked_examples.label: Example 16.4
worked_examples.method: Compare with the Euclidean plane; compute circumference 2 pi a xi over proper radius a xi.
worked_examples.key_insight: Flat slices obey Euclid: parallels stay parallel, angle sums are pi, and the ratio is exactly 2 pi.

worked_examples.label: Example 16.5
worked_examples.method: Use the 2-sphere as the model: meeting parallels, angle excess via Girard's theorem; compute circumference over proper radius with l = a arcsin xi.
worked_examples.key_insight: Since arcsin xi exceeds xi, circles are shorter than Euclid predicts, the hallmark of positive curvature.
worked_examples.result: Ratio = 2 pi xi / arcsin xi <= 2 pi.

worked_examples.label: Example 16.6
worked_examples.problem: Interpret the angle-like radial coordinate of the closed universe for light propagation.
worked_examples.method: Treat chi as an angle on a circle and follow radial light rays around it (Fig. 16.4).
worked_examples.key_insight: A closed space lets light from one source arrive by two routes and, in principle, lets you see your own back, though realistic models run out of time (Chapter 19). The example also reminds the reader that with a growing a(t) the proper separation of fixed comoving points on the circle keeps increasing.

worked_examples.label: Example 16.7
worked_examples.method: Hyperbolic model: diverging parallels, Lambert's area formula read as a sphere of imaginary radius, Poincaré disc picture; compute circumference over radius with l = a arsinh xi.
worked_examples.key_insight: arsinh xi is smaller than xi, so circles are longer than Euclid predicts: negative curvature.
worked_examples.result: Ratio = 2 pi xi / arsinh xi >= 2 pi.

worked_examples.label: Example 16.8
worked_examples.problem: Relate the observed period of light from a distant comoving galaxy to the emitted period.
worked_examples.method: Integrate the radial null condition for two crests; equate since the comoving distance is the same; split the time integrals and cancel the common part; approximate 1/a as constant over one period.
worked_examples.key_insight: The comoving distance light covers in one period at emission equals that at reception, so periods scale with a.
worked_examples.result: delta t_em / a(t_em) = delta t_ob / a(t_ob), hence omega_ob/omega_em = a(t_em)/a(t_ob).
concepts: radial null geodesic in a Robertson–Walker spacetime

worked_examples.label: Example 16.9
worked_examples.problem: Decide the sign of the shift for expanding and contracting universes, including light around the closed universe of Fig. 16.4.
worked_examples.method: Apply eqn 16.46 with a(t_ob) larger or smaller than a(t_em).
worked_examples.key_insight: Only the ratio of scale factors matters, not the route or distance; expansion reddens, contraction blues.

worked_examples.problem: Obtain the spatial Ricci tensor and scalar from the constant-curvature Riemann tensor.
worked_examples.method: Contract eqn 16.2 with gamma^ik using gamma^ik gamma_ik = 3 (margin eqn 16.3), then contract again.
worked_examples.key_insight: In n dimensions the factor would be (n-1)K; in 3D it is 2K, and the scalar is 6K.

worked_examples.problem: Compute the total proper volume of a k = +1 spatial slice.
worked_examples.method: Integrate the shell volume 4 pi (a sin chi)^2 a dchi over 0 <= chi <= pi.
worked_examples.key_insight: The bounded range of chi turns the angular coordinate range into finite volume without any boundary.

worked_examples.problem: Express the frequency result as a redshift parameter.
worked_examples.method: Convert omega ratio to wavelength ratio, define z, and set a(t_ob) = 1.
worked_examples.key_insight: Measuring z directly measures the scale factor at emission relative to today.
concepts: wavelength stretching with the scale factor

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Pressing a curved skin flat: a positively curved cap (like a ball) must tear, a negatively curved patch (a saddle is our example; the book just says negative curvature) must overlap and fold
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Opening margin note sets up the idea that positive curvature makes circles too short and negative curvature too long; §16.2 explicitly reuses it for all three RW spaces.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Uses 2D surfaces seen from outside; the 3D slices must be diagnosed intrinsically with spheres or circles inside them.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Peel a spherical cap and a saddle patch onto a plane in an animation, showing gaps or overlaps, then show the corresponding circle ratio.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A sphere's Gaussian curvature is 1/r^2, so a(t) is 'the radius of the universe'
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Justifies calling the length-valued scale factor a radius after the rescaling K = k/a^2.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Meaningful only for k = +1; for k = 0 a has no geometric size and the 'radius' of a hyperbolic space is imaginary in this sense.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Two-dimensional creatures living on a globe's surface can find no middle and no rim
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Explains why a finite-volume closed universe has neither boundary nor centre; those only appear from the fictitious embedding space.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The embedding picture itself suggests a centre inside the ball, which the analogy must then disown.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Flatland walker on a sphere: first-person view where walking straight always returns to the start and every point looks the same.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The radial coordinate of a closed universe is like an angle around a circle; light can lap the universe and let you see the back of your own head
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Example 16.6 with Fig. 16.4 makes the topology of the 3-sphere concrete through light propagation.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: A margin note says realistic expanding models do not allow enough time for a full lap; the circle picture suppresses two dimensions.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Animated photon lapping a circle universe with an expansion-history slider showing whether the lap completes.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Lambert's hyperbolic area formula is Girard's spherical formula for a sphere of imaginary radius
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Presents negative curvature as the analytic continuation of positive curvature, R^2 -> -R^2, and sin -> sinh.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Formal; no actual surface with imaginary radius exists in Euclidean space.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Slider for curvature K from positive through zero to negative with Sigma(chi) morphing from sin to chi to sinh and triangle angle sums updating.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The Poincaré disc as a shadow of the hyperboloid
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Fig. 16.5 shows the infinite hyperbolic sheet squeezed into a finite disc by projection.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Distances are badly distorted near the rim; only angles are faithful.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A photon's wavelength is frozen into space and stretches with it
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: wavelength stretching with the scale factor
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Rereads the frequency result as a stretching of the wave pattern by the factor a(t_ob)/a(t_em).
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Can suggest that all lengths (atoms, galaxies, rulers) stretch, or that the redshift is caused locally by space pulling on photons; bound systems do not expand.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Sine wave drawn on a stretching rubber strip with a comoving grid, next to an atom that keeps its size.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A ruler big enough to measure the expansion would expand with it
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Motivates why redshift, not direct length measurement, is the observable.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Physically misleading as stated: rigid bound rulers do not follow the Hubble flow; the real problem is that we cannot lay a ruler over cosmological distances at an instant of cosmic time.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Robertson–Walker metric is a solution of Einstein's equation.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Its form follows from homogeneity and isotropy alone; Einstein's equation with matter only determines a(t) and relates k to content (Chapter 17).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Most metrics met earlier (e.g. Schwarzschild) were derived by solving the field equations.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: If space is flat (k = 0) then spacetime is flat.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: With a time-dependent a(t) the spacetime Riemann tensor is non-zero; only constant a gives Minkowski space.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The word flat is used for the k = 0 case without qualification.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The spatial curvature quantities (3)R_ij = 2K gamma_ij go straight into Einstein's equation.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They describe only the slices; Einstein's equation needs the four-dimensional Ricci tensor, which also contains adot and addot terms.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Both are called Ricci tensors and look similar.
concepts: connection coefficients of the Robertson–Walker metric

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Constant spatial curvature means the spacetime has constant curvature.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: RW slices have constant curvature at each time, but the spacetime generally does not; de Sitter is a special case where it does.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The phrase 'space of constant curvature' is used for both.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A closed (finite) universe must have an edge or a centre.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A 3-sphere is finite yet boundaryless and homogeneous; the centre of the embedding ball is not part of the universe.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Every finite object in everyday life has a boundary, and embedding pictures show a ball with a middle.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: 'Open universe' means the k = -1 case only.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Both k = 0 and k = -1 have infinite volume; the book therefore prefers the terms flat and hyperbolic.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Older literature pairs open/flat/closed with k = -1/0/+1.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The whole hyperbolic space can be drawn as a surface in ordinary Euclidean space.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only pieces can; the full space needs a Minkowski ambient space or a model such as the Poincaré disc.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Saddle surfaces look like hyperbolic geometry.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: In a closed universe you really could see the back of your own head.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It is geometrically possible in a static closed space, but in physically realistic models light does not have time to go around (Chapter 19).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The geometric picture of Fig. 16.4(b) seems to guarantee it.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Cosmological redshift is just a Doppler shift from galaxies moving through space.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It is a distinct effect fixed entirely by a(t_em)/a(t_ob) for comoving sources, not by a relative velocity at any instant; the book lists it as a third cause of redshift.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Hubble's law reads like a velocity law, and small-z redshifts match v/c.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Redshift is set directly by the source's distance or by the route the light takes.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The shift is fixed by the scale factor at the emission and reception events alone. Distance and route matter only because they determine how long ago the light left (t_em); two sources at different distances whose light left at the same cosmic time show the same z, and light reaching A by the long and short routes of Fig. 16.4(a) is reddened according to its own emission time.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Hubble's law implies nothing can recede faster than light.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: v_p = H d_p is a rate of change of proper distance on a slice, not a local velocity; it exceeds c beyond d_p = c/H without contradicting relativity.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: It is written as a velocity.
concepts: proper distance in a Robertson–Walker spacetime

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Everything, including atoms, planets and rulers, expands with the universe.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only systems not bound together follow the Hubble flow; bound systems keep their size, which is exactly what lets us compare wavelengths.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter's ruler remark and the stretched-wavelength picture suggest universal stretching.
concepts: wavelength stretching with the scale factor

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Big Bang was an explosion at a point in a pre-existing space.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: a -> 0 everywhere at once; every point of an infinite k = 0 or -1 universe is at the singularity, which is a boundary of spacetime rather than an event inside space.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter's opening talks of geometries shrinking to a point.

thought_experiments.name: Seeing the back of your own head
thought_experiments.setup: In a closed universe, light scattered backwards off your head travels radially all the way around the chi circle and returns to your eyes.
thought_experiments.lesson: The 3-sphere is finite and edgeless; straight lines close on themselves, but real expansion histories limit this.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Animated lap of a photon on an expanding circle universe with a completion meter.

thought_experiments.name: Two crests from a distant galaxy
thought_experiments.setup: A comoving galaxy emits two successive wave crests separated by one period; both travel along radial null rays to a comoving observer.
thought_experiments.lesson: Equal comoving distances force the received period to be stretched by a(t_ob)/a(t_em).
concepts: radial null geodesic in a Robertson–Walker spacetime
thought_experiments.app_idea: Spacetime diagram with shaded 1/a areas for the two rays (see Fig. 16.6 redesign).

thought_experiments.name: Measuring circles in the universe
thought_experiments.setup: Galaxies at fixed comoving radius xi from us form a circle; compare its measured circumference with its measured radius.
thought_experiments.lesson: The ratio relative to 2 pi reveals the sign of spatial curvature from inside.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Circle-growing tool on sphere, plane, and hyperbolic disc with a ratio meter.

thought_experiments.name: Measuring expansion with a ruler
thought_experiments.setup: Try to measure cosmic expansion by laying a gigantic ruler between galaxies.
thought_experiments.lesson: Direct length measurement at an instant is impossible in practice; the accessible observable is the frequency shift of light.
concepts: proper distance in a Robertson–Walker spacetime

thought_experiments.name: Running the expanding universe backwards
thought_experiments.setup: Follow a matter-filled expanding model back in time as the density rises.
thought_experiments.lesson: a reaches zero a finite time ago; density and curvature diverge and the classical description must stop.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Reverse-time animation of comoving grid shrinking with a curvature-scalar gauge heading to infinity.

historical_notes.event: Showed that the constant-curvature metric in eqn 16.5 is the only metric compatible with homogeneity and isotropy (the book gives no date; historically their work dates to 1935-1936).
historical_notes.significance: Establishes that cosmology on large scales has only three geometric options, labelled by k.

historical_notes.event: Spherical triangle area formula (angle excess), recalled from Chapter 3.
One of several independent discoverers of hyperbolic geometry, which is sometimes named after him.
historical_notes.significance: Provides the geometry of the k = -1 universe; margin note adds the Tom Lehrer song anecdote.

historical_notes.event: Formula for the area of a hyperbolic triangle from its angle deficit.
Beltrami formulated the disc model of hyperbolic geometry; Poincaré rediscovered it fourteen years later and it bears his name.
historical_notes.significance: Conformal representation of hyperbolic space used in Figs 16.3(b) and 16.5, and a precursor of the conformal methods of Chapter 19.

historical_notes.event: Satirical song about Lobachevsky, with Lehrer noting the name was chosen for its rhythm.
historical_notes.significance: Humorous aside humanizing the history of non-Euclidean geometry.

historical_notes.significance: Sets the tone that on large scales the universe is featureless, i.e. homogeneous and isotropic.

applications_and_observations.topic: Redshift as the observable of cosmic expansion
applications_and_observations.details: Measuring z for a source gives the ratio of today's scale factor to the scale factor when the light left, so a catalogue of redshifts (with independent distance or time information) maps out a(t).
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: 1+z = a(t_ob)/a(t_em); with a(t_ob) = 1, a(t_em) = 1/(1+z). Own illustration: the cosmic microwave background at z about 1100 was emitted when the universe was about 1/1100 of its present linear size.

applications_and_observations.topic: Hubble's law in curved RW universes
applications_and_observations.details: The proportionality of recession rate to proper distance holds in all three geometries, so Hubble's observed linear law does not by itself determine k.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: v_p = H d_p with H = adot/a. Own estimate: for H_0 about 70 km/s/Mpc, v_p reaches c at d_p = c/H_0 of roughly 4.3 Gpc.

applications_and_observations.topic: Finite size of a closed universe
applications_and_observations.details: A k = +1 universe of radius a has volume 2 pi^2 a^3, and the greatest proper distance from any point (the antipode) is pi a.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: V = 2 pi^2 a^3 (about 19.7 a^3); antipodal distance pi a; the areal coordinate r reaches 1 at proper distance pi a/2.

applications_and_observations.topic: Redshift of neutrinos and gravitational waves
applications_and_observations.details: The wavelength-proportional-to-a scaling applies not only to photons but also to cosmological neutrinos and gravitational waves.

applications_and_observations.topic: Redshift drift as a probe of expansion history
applications_and_observations.details: Exercise 16.9 shows that the rate of change of a source's redshift with observer time encodes the expansion rate at emission relative to today.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Signature (-, +, +, +) with c = 1; the RW line element begins -dt^2.
A left superscript (3) marks tensors built from the spatial 3-metric of a constant-t slice, e.g. (3)R_ijkl, (3)R.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Latin indices i, j, k, l run over spatial coordinates; Greek over spacetime.

notation_and_conventions.convention: gamma_ij is the comoving spatial metric without the a^2 factor; the full spatial metric components are a^2 gamma_ij.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The curvature K in (3)R_ijkl refers to gamma_ij, so after rescaling the physical curvature of a slice is k/a^2.

notation_and_conventions.convention: K is the dimensional Gaussian curvature (1/length^2); k in {+1, 0, -1} its sign after rescaling; C is used for the constant in a constant-curvature spacetime to avoid confusion with K.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Many texts call C by K as well.

notation_and_conventions.convention: a(t) starts dimensionless and is redefined as a length (a/sqrt|K|) for k = ±1, making r dimensionless; later normalizations set a(t_ob) = 1.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Mixed conventions within the book: dimensionful a here versus a(today) = 1 in the redshift margin note.

notation_and_conventions.convention: After rescaling, r-bar is written simply as r.

notation_and_conventions.item: Radial coordinates r, R, chi, xi
notation_and_conventions.convention: R isotropic radius; r areal (circumference) radius; chi hyperspherical radius with r = Sigma(chi); xi a fixed comoving value of r for a particular galaxy.
notation_and_conventions.notes: In §16.3 the source is placed at 'r = chi', using chi as a label for the r value while the upper limit of the integral is written chi; a learner may confuse this with the chi coordinate.

notation_and_conventions.convention: sin chi, chi, sinh chi for k = +1, 0, -1.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Other books write S_k(chi) or f_k(chi).

notation_and_conventions.convention: phi runs from -pi to pi; chi from 0 to pi for k = +1 and 0 to infinity otherwise.
Hats denote orthonormal-frame components obtained with vielbeins (e_mu)^{mu-hat}.
l(t) or d_p for proper distance, v_p = dl/dt for proper velocity; exercises use a script ell with subscripts em and ob.
t_em, t_ob emission and observation times; eta denotes the comoving distance integral of dt/a.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Elsewhere eta often denotes conformal time.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Universe 0 and Universe 1 (de Sitter) refer to the spatially flat toy models of Chapter 15.
The book prefers spherical/flat/hyperbolic over closed/flat/open for k = +1/0/-1.
Here t_0 labels the moment at which a(t) vanishes (the initial singularity), and the text also mentions choosing the time origin so that a(0) = 0.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Many cosmology texts, and later usage, reserve t_0 for the present epoch; flag the clash so learners do not read t_0 as 'today'.

margin_notes.summary: Constant curvature means the same curvature everywhere, captured by one number; pointer to Exercises 16.5 and 15.3.
Reminder that circles on a ball have circumference below 2 pi r (flattening tears), while negatively curved surfaces have circles above 2 pi r (flattening folds).
The spatial curvature can only be built from gamma_ij or the Levi-Civita symbol; any other tensor would pick a direction, and in fact gamma_ij alone suffices.
Boxed pointer: Gaussian curvature is treated fully in Chapter 30; for now K is simply a constant labelling the geometry classes.
Contraction computation gamma^ik(gamma_ik gamma_jl - gamma_il gamma_jk) = 2 gamma_jl.
Caution: the spatial Ricci expressions are not the spacetime ones used in Einstein's equation.
Constant spatial curvature differs from constant spacetime curvature (de Sitter, R_mu nu = R g_mu nu/4); the equivalent Riemann form with constant C is given and linked to the exercises.
Margin list for the RW metric in r form: metric components, vielbein, all non-zero connection coefficients, orthonormal Ricci components and Ricci scalar.
Appendix D shows r = sin chi (k = 1), r = sinh chi (k = -1), r = chi (k = 0) simplify the metric.
Margin list for the chi form: metric components and vielbein.
Comoving coordinates must satisfy g_00,i = g_0i,0 = 0, which RW coordinates do.
Boxed pointer: classical curvature of spherical, flat and hyperbolic spaces is in Chapter 30; embedding in Appendix D.
Explicit embedding of the k = 1 slice as a sphere in 4D Euclidean space (eqn 16.28).
Realistic models do not leave enough time for light to circle the universe; shown in Chapter 19.
Explicit hyperboloid embedding of the k = -1 slice (eqn 16.33); only parts of the space embed in Euclidean space.
Hyperbolic geometry references (Penrose 2004, Needham 1997), multiple discoverers, Lobachevsky, and the Tom Lehrer song anecdote.
Lambert's life dates.
The Poincaré disc is conformal (Chapter 19); it was first formulated by Beltrami in 1868 and rediscovered by Poincaré later; see Penrose for history.
Terminology caution: open/flat/closed is ambiguous because the flat case is also open; the book uses hyperbolic/flat/spherical.
Boxed pointer: gravitational redshift from climbing out of a potential is discussed in Chapter 22.
Defines the time-independent comoving distance eta (eqn 16.37), contrasted with the growing proper distance a eta.
The wavelength-scales-with-a property also applies to neutrinos and gravitational waves.
With a(t_ob) = 1 the redshift relation becomes 1+z = 1/a(t_em).

notable.summary: Carry out the substitution from the isotropic polar radius to the areal radius and confirm the dr^2/(1-Kr^2) form.

notable.summary: Multi-part derivation proving uniqueness: start from a general spherically symmetric 3-metric with g_rr = e^{2 Lambda}, find orthonormal Riemann and Ricci components, impose Ricci = 2K times the metric, and solve to recover dr^2/(1-Kr^2).
notable.why_notable: Turns the chapter's quoted Robertson–Walker uniqueness into a proof; note the printed R_rr and the constant-curvature conditions contain typos (factor 2 and exponent).

notable.summary: Show that if a spacetime's Riemann tensor has the maximally symmetric form at every point, the coefficient cannot vary from place to place, using the contracted Bianchi identity and metric compatibility.
notable.why_notable: A version of Schur's theorem, justifying why isotropy everywhere implies homogeneity of curvature.

notable.summary: Contract the maximally symmetric Riemann form to get Ricci proportional to the metric with factor 1/4 in four dimensions, and generalize to d dimensions.

notable.summary: Given a galaxy's redshift and its present proper distance, find its proper distance when the light was emitted.
notable.why_notable: Quick check that comoving separations scale with a, giving a factor 1/(1+z).

notable.summary: Differentiate the redshift relation with respect to observer time, accounting for how emission time changes, to express the past expansion rate through today's rate, z and its drift.

difficulty.notes: The symmetry argument and the transformations are short but lean on unproved assertions (uniqueness of the Riemann form and of the metric) and on Appendix D and Chapter 30 for geometry. The three-case tour is gentle and pictorial; the redshift derivation is clean. Stumbling blocks are the multiplicity of radial coordinates (R, r, chi, xi, and chi used as an r value), the change in the meaning and dimensions of a(t) mid-chapter, and several printed typos in margin formulas and in Exercise 16.4. Component lists appear without derivation.
