teaching_gems.gem: Decide what the curvature tensor must look like from symmetry before searching for any metric.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows learners that the three cosmological geometries are forced by the cosmological principle, not chosen, and gives a template (symmetry fixes tensor form) that recurs throughout physics.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Tensor 'symmetry filter': learners toggle candidate building blocks (gamma_ij, a vector n_i, epsilon_ijk) and see which survive rotations and Riemann symmetries, leaving the single K structure.

teaching_gems.gem: Pick the radial coordinate so that circumferences come out as 2 pi a r.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Coordinate choice becomes a physical demand rather than an algebra trick, and it explains why curvature then shows up only in g_rr.
teaching_gems.app_idea: On a sphere, drag a circle and display three candidate radii (isotropic R, areal r, arc length chi) with the circumference; learners see which label matches 2 pi r.

teaching_gems.gem: One number, circumference over radius compared with 2 pi, distinguishes all three geometries.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Reduces an abstract classification to a measurement a learner could imagine doing with galaxies.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Three side-by-side worlds with a shared radius slider and a ratio gauge that dips below, sits at, or rises above 2 pi.

teaching_gems.gem: Hyperbolic formulas are spherical formulas with an imaginary radius (Girard -> Lambert, sin -> sinh).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Unifies the three cases under a single curvature parameter, so learners remember one formula family instead of three.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Continuous curvature slider from +1/R^2 through 0 to -1/R^2 driving Sigma(chi), triangle angle sums, and volume growth plots.

teaching_gems.gem: Treat the closed universe's radial coordinate as an angle, so light can lap the universe and show you your own back.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A vivid, slightly absurd image fixes the topology of the 3-sphere in memory, and the margin caveat invites a later payoff.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Photon-lap animation on an expanding circle with a 'did it make it?' result depending on a(t).

teaching_gems.gem: Split the two null-ray integrals so the long shared interval cancels, leaving one period at each end.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Turns an apparently global calculation into a local comparison, and the timing diagram makes the cancellation visible.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Area-under-1/a spacetime diagram with two draggable emission times and live cancellation shading.

teaching_gems.gem: Redshift depends only on a at emission and at observation: the wavelength is stretched with space.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives an instantly usable rule (1+z = a_ob/a_em) and a picture that transfers to neutrinos and gravitational waves.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Wave on a stretching grid, with a photon, a neutrino wave packet and a GW strain pattern all scaling identically.

teaching_gems.gem: Flat space is not flat spacetime: k = 0 with a changing a is curved.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Pre-empts a persistent confusion about 'flat universe' language and connects directly to the Ricci scalar formula.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Curvature readout panel showing (3)R and the 4D Ricci scalar separately as the learner changes k and the expansion history.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed margin Ricci component R_ii-hat ends with 2k/a; it must be 2k/a^2 (dimensions, and consistency with the stated Ricci scalar).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Anyone deriving the Friedmann equations from the margin list gets a dimensionally inconsistent curvature term.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show the corrected component and verify -R_tt + 3R_ii = R as a check.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 16.4: printed R_rr = Lambda'/r should be 2 Lambda'/r, so the first condition in (d) should be Lambda' = Kr e^{2 Lambda}; the second condition prints e^{-Lambda} where e^{-2 Lambda} is needed.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Following the printed equations does not lead to the stated answer dr^2/(1-Kr^2), causing confusion about what went wrong.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Provide corrected equations; check with Lambda = -ln(1-Kr^2)/2.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. 16.6 caption writes the second observation time as t_ob + delta t_em (should be delta t_ob) and 'comment' for 'common'.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Suggests periods are unchanged, contradicting the result being derived.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Label the diagram with delta t_ob and highlight that it differs from delta t_em.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The claims that eqn 16.2 is the only possible arrangement and that 16.5 is the only matching metric are asserted, not derived, in the text.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may accept the uniqueness without understanding the role of isotropy about every point (Schur's theorem) or of local vs global uniqueness.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Point to Exercises 16.4-16.5 and mention that topology is not fixed by local geometry.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The areal coordinate r for k = +1 only covers half the 3-sphere (r = sin chi reaches 1 at the equator); g_rr diverges at r = 1 and Fig. 16.1 stops there.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The finite limit pi a/2 in Example 16.3 can be mistaken for the size of the universe, and the divergence for a physical singularity.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Prefer the chi form for global statements; show that the maximum proper distance is pi a.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: At the start of §16.2 the text recalls l(t) = a xi for a galaxy at coordinate xi, which is only the k = 0 result.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Makes the circumference-to-radius comparison look trivially equal to 2 pi for all k.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State that the circumference is 2 pi a xi in all cases while the proper radius depends on k.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Setting K = 0 is said to give 'the flat spacetime of the de Sitter model'; in fact it gives the spatially flat RW family with arbitrary a(t), of which de Sitter (exponential a) is one case and which is curved spacetime unless a is constant.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Mixes spatial and spacetime flatness and ties the flat case to one specific expansion law.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say 'spatially flat metric of the form used for Universe 1'.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: In §16.3 the source is placed at 'r = chi' and the integrals use chi as their upper limit, while chi is also the hyperspherical coordinate whose value is the integral itself.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Notation collision obscures that the comoving distance eta equals the chi coordinate of the source.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Call the source's areal coordinate r_1 and write eta = chi(r_1).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The ruler argument for why expansion cannot be measured directly implies measuring devices expand; bound objects do not follow the Hubble flow.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Reinforces the misconception that everything expands, which would make redshift undetectable.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Replace with: proper distances live on a constant-time slice that no observer can survey; only light signals connect us to distant galaxies.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The redshift derivation silently assumes comoving source and observer and uses coordinate time as proper time (g_tt = -1); peculiar velocities and the combination with Doppler shifts are not discussed.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may apply 1+z = a_ob/a_em to objects with large peculiar motions or wonder why t can be used as a clock.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State the assumptions explicitly and note that total redshift multiplies (1+z_total) = (1+z_cos)(1+z_pec).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Closed/open is equated with k = +1 versus k <= 0, and the opening says the geometries 'shrink to a point'; topology and dynamics are conflated with local geometry.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think flat universes must be infinite, or that the singularity is a point in space.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Mention that flat or hyperbolic spaces can be compactified, and that a -> 0 happens everywhere simultaneously; whether it happens depends on the Friedmann dynamics, not the metric form.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Hubble's law via proper velocity is given without noting superluminal recession beyond c/H or the distinction from measured velocities.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Common confusion about faster-than-light recession and about interpreting redshift as velocity.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a short note and a numerical example with the Hubble distance.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The k = -1 slice is described (main text and Example 16.2) as a '2-sheet hyperboloid'; the spatial universe is a single sheet of the two-sheeted surface w^2 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2 = a^2, as Fig. 16.2(b) correctly draws.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A learner may picture two disconnected copies of space, or think the open universe has two components.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say 'one sheet (w > 0) of a two-sheeted hyperboloid' and point to the single bowl in Fig. 16.2(b).

tutor_notes: Open with: 'If the universe looks the same everywhere and in every direction, how many different shapes could space have?' Let the learner guess before revealing the answer: three, labelled by the sign of one curvature number.
Check that the learner remembers from Chapter 15 why the metric has the -dt^2 + a^2 gamma_ij form; emphasize that no field equation has been used yet.

Teach the three geometries in 2D first (sphere, plane, saddle or Poincaré disc) using circles and triangles, then promote to 3D by analogy. Ask: 'On a sphere, is a circle's circumference bigger or smaller than 2 pi times its radius measured along the surface?'

Keep the radial coordinates straight explicitly: R (isotropic), r (areal, circumference-defined), chi (proper radial distance divided by a), xi (a particular galaxy's r). Write r = Sigma(chi) on the board and return to it whenever confusion arises.
When a(t) changes from dimensionless to a length, flag it: after rescaling the curvature of a slice is k/a^2, so a genuinely is a radius of curvature for k = +1.
Check understanding with: 'Is a k = 0 universe with growing a(t) curved?' The correct answer is that space is flat but spacetime is curved; point to the addot and adot terms in the Ricci scalar.

For the redshift, draw the two-ray timing picture first and ask the learner to identify which time interval is shared; then let them write delta t/a = constant themselves. Follow up: 'Does the path or the distance enter the final formula?'
Use a numerical anchor: if light left when the universe was half its present size, z = 1; the CMB at z of about 1100 left when distances were about 1100 times smaller (own illustration).

Anticipate the questions 'Can galaxies recede faster than light?', 'Does my ruler expand?', and 'Where did the Big Bang happen?' and answer with the proper-distance-on-a-slice idea, bound systems, and a -> 0 everywhere at once.
Warn about the printed typos (margin Ricci 2k/a, Exercise 16.4 R_rr and exponent, Fig. 16.6 caption) before learners use those formulas.
For advanced learners, connect the Ricci components here to the Friedmann equations of Chapter 17 and have them verify the trace R = -R_tt + 3R_ii.
For beginners, skip the connection coefficient list and Exercise 16.4; the essential takeaways are the metric with k, proper distance and Hubble's law, the three geometries, and 1+z = a_ob/a_em.
